posts.title: Ep 71 Acute Pulmonary Edema
posts.postText:
#TBT: a 2016 Core EM classic, remastered.

The first 10 minutes of acute pulmonary edema with Anand Swaminathan:

1) look, don't listen (B-lines beat the stethoscope)
2) get NIPPV on the patient immediately
3) nitrates unload preload and afterload
4) find the cause

Since this lecture is from 2016, the diuretic and nitrate guidance is updated on screen to current HF guidelines.

posts.title: Ep 222 LAST
posts.postText:
2 minutes on local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST).

Metallic taste. Seizures. A wide QRS or arrest after a block or lidocaine. Think LAST.

Stop the injection and get lipid 20% early: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min.

Arrest? Modified ACLS: low-dose epi, amiodarone, no more lidocaine.

Core EM Ep 222.

posts.title: Ep 212 Angioedema
posts.postText:
#TBT Core EM Ep 212 (2025): Angioedema with Dr. Maria Mulligan-Buckmiller and host Brian Gilberti.

Airway first. Make sure the airway is secure, they're controlling their secretions, and the airway is patent. Watch for stridor, labored breathing, a sensation of throat closure, and trouble breathing or talking.

If it's histamine-mediated, epi is lifesaving.

No hives and no itching should make you think bradykinin, like hereditary angioedema. In Mia's case, there was no redness and no itching, it had happened in her dad, and she had been off her prescribed medicine for a year.

ACE inhibitors are a frequent trigger for bradykinin-mediated angioedema. In rare situations, ARBs are also the culprits.

Trust your clinical judgment. Labs and imaging often help with downstream care, not the initial decision.

Targeted HAE treatments are covered in the full episode at coreem.net (link in bio)
#FOAMed #EmergencyMedicine #MedEd #TBT #Angioedema

posts.title: Ep 220 Post-ROSC
posts.postText:
#TBT Core EM Ep 220 (2026): Post-ROSC Care
with Dr. Jonathan Elmer and host Brian Gilberti.

ROSC isn't the finish line.

Expect the crash, and be ready.
The epi we gave during the code wears off, so have a push-dose pressor at the bedside.

Don't anchor on ischemic-looking EKG changes.
They may be a consequence of the arrest.
Cast a broad net.

The stunned brain often looks bleak in the first minutes or hours.
It often gets better with time.

Bring the family to the bedside if they're willing.
When asked about prognosis, it's okay to say I don't know.

posts.title: Ep 223 Thyroid Storm
posts.postText:
Thyroid storm has no lab cutoff.
Altered mentation is the tell.

PTU first. Wait at least an hour. Then iodine.
Steroids and high-dose propranolol block T4 to T3 conversion.
Fever? Acetaminophen. Never aspirin.

posts.title: Ep 218 SCAPE
posts.postText:
#TBT Core EM Ep 218 (2026): SCAPE
with Naz Sarpoulaki and host Brian Gilberti.

SCAPE is a maldistribution problem, not necessarily volume overload.
Wet lungs, maybe a dry tank.

Don't wait for the x-ray.
Bilateral B-lines on bedside ultrasound in a hypertensive, dyspneic patient point firmly to it, in seconds.

Start BiPAP or CPAP immediately when appropriate.

Then high-dose nitro for arterial dilation, roughly 100 to 150 mcg/min and up as described in the episode.

Ask about phosphodiesterase inhibitors first, since they're a contraindication.

Truly overloaded? Consider IV diuretics after stabilizing.
They take time.

Vasodilators fix the pipes, and in SCAPE the pipes are the immediate problem.

Avoid morphine and beta blockers when possible.

posts.title: Ep 229 Iron Poisoning #TBT
posts.postText:
#TBT Core EM Ep 229 (2026): Iron Poisoning
with Dr. Brian Chastain and host Brian Gilberti.

The latent phase is a dangerous trap.
They can look like they're turning the corner right before they crump.

Improvement in GI symptoms doesn't mean the toxic effects have run their course.
Iron is being absorbed, and cardiovascular collapse and shock can follow.

Treat the patient, not the number.
If they're in shock or have a profound metabolic acidosis, start deferoxamine even if the serum iron level hasn't peaked or is lower than expected.
There's little harm other than hypotension.

It's the elemental iron dose, not the mass of the pill.
Ferrous sulfate has roughly 65 mg of elemental iron per 325 mg pill.
Under 20 mg/kg is usually asymptomatic.
Over 60 mg/kg is the threshold for serious toxicity and possible death.

Get an X-ray.
If you see pills on KUB, reach for whole bowel irrigation.
Skip the charcoal, and hold off on routine lavage.
Get poison control on the line early.

posts.title: Ep 214 Acute Pulmonary Embolism
posts.postText:
#TBT Core EM Ep 214 (2025): Acute PE
with Dr. Vivian Chiu and host Brian Gilberti.

PE is a master of disguise, from subtle shortness of breath to collapse.

Keep a broad differential:
• pneumonia
• ACS
• pneumothorax
• heart failure exacerbation
• aortic dissection

Alarm bells for high-risk PE:
• SBP under 90 for over 15 minutes
• needing vasopressors
• signs of shock

Call your PERT team.

For low or intermediate risk, a negative D-dimer lets you skip the CT radiation.
High risk goes straight to imaging.

Troponin and BNP gauge RV strain and severity, not the diagnosis.

The RV despises big swings:
• skimp on fluids if you can
• lead with norepinephrine for low pressure
• avoid intubation when possible, since positive pressure can worsen RV dysfunction

Don't anchor on the obvious.
Always risk stratify and resuscitate with precision.

Ep 223 Thyroid Storm
posts.postText:
#TBT Core EM Ep 223 (2026): Thyroid Storm.

Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis.

Altered mentation is often what separates it from compensated thyrotoxicosis.

Order matters:
• PTU first
• wait at least an hour
• then iodine

Block T4 to T3 with propranolol, PTU, and steroids.

They are volume-down, so give crystalloid.

Cool with acetaminophen, never aspirin.
